newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS - Bad weather, slow reforms hit Kazakh harvest.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bad weather, slow reforms hit Kazakh harvest.

text.p: Bad weather and a string of difficulties along Kazakhstan's rocky path to a market economy hit the vast Central Asian nation's grain harvest for a second year in a row and output totalled only 11.6 million tonnes.
"The total bunker weight (for 1996) was 13.2 million tonnes while the cleaned weight was 11.6 million tonnes," Deputy Prime Minister Zhanybek Karibzhanov told a news conference on Monday.
Kazakh officials have been revising harvest forecasts downwards over the year. Early predictions put the harvest at 18 million tonnes, but this had fallen to 13-14 million in September.
This year's total was little better than last year's drought-hit harvest of 10 million tonnes.
"The harvest was carried out in very difficult conditions, and rain and snow in September and October hampered operations," said Karibzhanov, who is in charge of agriculture policy.
He confirmed farmers' gripes of a lack of machinery and spare parts, particularly of combine harvesters.
Karibzhanov said some 1.5 million hectares in western Kazakhstan, out of a total 17 million hectares sown to grains, were lost to drought.
But some officials and analysts dispute the official grain harvest data, saying farmers hid a sizeable amount.
"I believe the real harvest could have been as high as 15 million tonnes," said Alexander Korablin, press secretary at Kazakhstan's Ministry of Agriculture.
He said farmers were unwilling to reveal their real harvest totals, particularly on smaller farms, as they feared they might be forced to sell to the state for prices below world levels.
"A lot of grain has already gone over the border (to Russia) to pay for fuel, spare parts and other needs," Korablin told Reuters. "It is a very porous border."
Fear of officialdom on Kazakh farms, many of them in a state of limbo between state ownership and the free market, harks back to days of forced requisitioning in the Soviet era.

Korablin said debts from last year's poor harvest hung over producers, made worse by lopsided futures contracts with fuel producers. "We've had to swap grain for fuel at throwaway prices," he complained.
Karibzhanov said farmers' debts to electricity producers totalled four billion tenge ($56 million) in 1996.
Specialists have said disruptions in electricity supplies from Russian producers caused some grain to spoil because it could not be dried and put into silos in time.
Western specialists said a lack of cheap loans had hit farmers this year, despite $165 million in credits the government said it gave out for this year's harvest.
"There's a huge shortage of credit," said one Western expert. "Farming will never take off in this country until that's sorted out."
Karibzhanov said he still expected the former Soviet republic to export 5.6 million tonnes of grain this year, up 55 percent from last year.

After its own poor harvest, Russia, which sourced 70 percent of its wheat and wheat flour imports from Kazakhstan over the 1995/1996 crop marketing year, is likely to be in the market for Kazakh grain.

But it will have to move quickly to compete with buyers from Kazakhstan's Central Asian neighbours. Grain harvests in the mostly desert nations of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan were way below target this year.
